I was safely up a tree.

questions.prompt: Find the words Seton uses for the bull’s face and eyes. What feeling do they create?
facilitatorNotes: Ears back, muzzle raised, nose curled, teeth showing, mane bristling, eyes blazing green: a picture of fury. “Half a ton of hate” sums it up. The details make the reader feel the danger, even though we know Seton is safe.
evidence: in his eyes there blazed a marvellous fire of changing opalescent green
with all the power of half a ton of hate

questions.prompt: What made Fossum’s adventure more dangerous than Seton’s, and what saved him?
facilitatorNotes: He was in an open valley with no tree. The click of the camera woke the bull, which ran straight at him, and he kept focusing until it was ten feet away. A snowdrift that held the man but not the elk saved him.
evidence: stood there quietly focussing his camera, till the bull was within ten feet
a deep snowdrift that would carry the man, and would not carry the Elk

questions.prompt: Seton praises Fossum’s “most amazing nerve.” Was it nerve, or foolishness? Use the story to explain.
facilitatorNotes: Both can be argued. Seton admires the steady, unshaken picture; but Fossum risked his life for a photograph and was saved by luck. Readers might compare Seton, who chose a tree first.
evidence: Fossum with the most amazing nerve
there is no sign of shake on landscape or on Elk

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the siren call (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice a storyteller’s feelings changing as he tells, and decide what he wants you to feel at the end.
readings.focus: Seton calls a moose so well with a home-made horn that his partner shoots it, and he never calls one again.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. The moose is the largest deer. The Kippewa country is lake and forest land in Quebec; the Hunting Moon is an old name for an autumn month. A moose caller imitates a cow (female) moose to draw a bull within range. Wattap is spruce root used to sew birch-bark; “bad medicine” and “hoodoo” mean bad luck. In old Greek stories a siren sang to lure sailors to their deaths; the Florentine assassins were hired killers in old Italy.
readings.contentNote: A moose is shot and dies. Seton uses “halfbreed,” an old and now offensive word for a person of mixed Indigenous and white ancestry.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Horns and Hoofs and Legs of Speed,” from “The Moose, the Biggest of All Deer” through “The Siren Call”; opens “The Moose is one of the fine animals that have responded magnificently to protection in…”; closes “…a Moose since, and that rifle has hung unused in its rack from that to the present day.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Seton say the moose “responded magnificently to protection”? What numbers support him?
facilitatorNotes: In the park they grew from about fifty in 1897 to about five hundred and fifty, and spread wherever the woods suited them. Protection alone was enough: “all they needed was a little help.”
evidence: from about fifty in 1897 to some five hundred and fifty to-day
But all they needed was a little help

questions.prompt: Seton sets out “in a spirit of half jest.” What does he do to show off, and what do the guides think of it?
facilitatorNotes: He makes a birch-bark horn the old way and draws dancing “hoodoo Moose” on it. The guides shake their heads and say no moose will come. The moose does come; the bad luck turns out to be of another kind.
evidence: I'll have to go out and show you men how to call a Moose.
Moose never come

questions.prompt: Why does Seton wait a full fifteen minutes between calls, and why does he check his watch?
facilitatorNotes: A cow that seems too eager scares the bull away, so there is an “etiquette” of waiting; and when you wait hard, a minute feels like twenty, so he cannot trust his guess. It shows his skill.
evidence: it is easy to spoil all by trying to go too fast
when one is waiting so hard, the minute is like twenty

questions.prompt: Who is Seton’s partner, and how does each person in the canoe feel when the moose dies?
facilitatorNotes: The partner is a woman, as “she” and “the fair killer” show; she has tears in her eyes. The guide sobs too, but from triumph. Seton finds it “so unlovely.” Three people, three different feelings.
evidence: There were tears in the eyes of the fair killer
and a different sob was heard at my elbow

questions.prompt: Seton compares himself to assassins who trapped a brave man by “crying like a woman.” Why is the comparison so harsh, and what does he decide?
facilitatorNotes: He feels he used the moose’s own love-call as a lie to lure it. “It is a proud thing to act a lie so cleverly” is bitter. He never called a moose again, and the rifle hung unused. He does not say all hunting is wrong; readers can discuss what exactly he regrets.
evidence: it is a proud thing to act a lie so cleverly
But I have never called a Moose since

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the vanished buffalo and the flashing antelope (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Test the limits of a writer’s claim, and notice when a story told to him becomes something he checked.
readings.focus: The buffalo fell from millions to a few hundred; Seton asks what protection can and cannot do.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. The buffalo is the American bison. A ruminant is an animal that chews the cud; a man-o’-war is a warship; a heliograph sends signals by flashing sunlight from a mirror. The mark [B] points to Seton’s footnote, which names another of his books. Buffalo-birds are cowbirds. Seton’s claim that the buffalo’s end was “inevitable” is his opinion: the great herds were shot mostly for their hides, and their loss also took away the living of the Plains nations who depended on them. Pronghorn, which Seton feared were doomed, now number in the hundreds of thousands.
readings.contentNote: Seton writes a Native American man’s words in broken English, as many writers of his time did.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Horns and Hoofs and Legs of Speed,” from “The Biggest of Our Game--The Buffalo” through “The Doomed Antelope and His Heliograph”; opens “"Yes, that's a buffalo-bird," said the old Indian, pointing to some black birds, with…”; closes “…have passed away. A small band is yet to be seen wintering on the prairie near Gardiner.”.

questions.prompt: Seton first thought the buffalo-bird story was “a lusty myth.” What did he find when he looked into it?
facilitatorNotes: The birds really did follow the buffalo, nested in the wool of fallen skulls and lined their nests with buffalo wool; he even knew of a crippled bird that spent a winter in a bull’s mane. The story “bore the searchlight”: it held up when tested.
evidence: But the tale bore the searchlight better than I thought.
roosted at night between the mighty horns

questions.prompt: Put Seton’s buffalo numbers in order. What story do they tell?
facilitatorNotes: Over 50,000,000 in 1500; 800 in 1895; about 3,000 when he wrote. In the park, valleys “black-speckled” twenty years before, thirty in 1900, two hundred now. A huge fall, then a small climb under protection.
evidence: I estimate them at over 50,000,000 in A.D. 1500. In 1895 they were down to 800
In 1900 the remnant in the Park had fallen to thirty

questions.prompt: Seton says the end of the great herds “was inevitable,” but also that “we brought it on forty or fifty years before it was necessary.” Do the two claims fit together? Is the first one proved?
facilitatorNotes: He means settlers would have pushed the herds out in the end, and admits people hurried it. But “inevitable” is an opinion, not a proved fact, and his own figures show protection bringing buffalo back. Readers can argue either way from the text.
evidence: it is well to remind the reader that it was inevitable
only we brought it on forty or fifty years before it was necessary

questions.prompt: What is the antelope’s “heliograph,” and what is it for?
facilitatorNotes: Muscles lift the white hair on its rump into a shining disc that flashes in the sun and shows for miles. It usually warns of danger and also helps antelope find each other, as when Seton saw two bands come together.
evidence: they can erect the white hair of the rump patch into a large, flat, snow-white disc
The flash is usually a signal of danger

questions.prompt: Why does Seton call the antelope “doomed” even though it was protected? Was he right?
facilitatorNotes: Its numbers in the park had fallen to a third in spite of protection, and he feared a law of nature was against it. He was wrong about the species: pronghorn recovered across the West. A careful prediction can still fail.
evidence: in spite of good protection, continue to go down

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: Old Silver-grizzle, the badger (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a writer who has changed his mind about an animal, and weigh his reasons.
readings.focus: Seton defends the badger, confesses how he once treated one, and explains its surprising friendships.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. A badger is a strong, low, digging animal of the plains. Dirigible means steerable, like an airship; a conceit here is a fanciful idea; “in ill odour” means disliked; gregarious means living in herds. The Saskatchewan and the Souris are rivers of the Canadian prairie, where Seton lived as a young man. “First endured, then pitied, then embraced” is borrowed from the poet Alexander Pope.
readings.contentNote: Seton calls Native Americans “redmen,” an old term now considered offensive. As a boy he and his companions killed a badger for its skin; he does not describe how.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Old Silver-grizzle--The Badger,” from the opening through “His Sociable Bent”; opens “A brilliant newspaper man once gave vast publicity to the story that at last a use had…”; closes “…Evidently it was a partnership founded on good-will, however it may have been begun.”.

questions.prompt: The chapter opens with a newspaper story about a “dirigible Badger” that digs post-holes. Was it true? Why might Seton begin with it?
facilitatorNotes: It was a joke or hoax, and Seton says he could disprove it. It leads to the one real complaint against badgers: holes that break horses’ legs and riders’ necks.
evidence: Unfortunately I was in a position to disprove this pretty conceit.
this indiscretion has made many enemies

questions.prompt: Seton calls the badger both “valiant” and “harmless.” Does his own description support both words?
facilitatorNotes: Valiant: the heart of a bulldog, the claws of a grizzly, brave to the last ditch. Harmless: it minds its own business if let alone and eats farm pests. It is not harmless to ground-squirrels, so “harmless” means harmless to people who leave it be.
evidence: He minds his own business, if let alone
he has the heart of a bulldog, the claws of a Grizzly, and the jaws of a small crocodile

questions.prompt: Compare Seton’s meeting with a badger in 1882 and his meeting in 1897. How had he changed?
facilitatorNotes: In 1882, as a boy, he grabbed a badger’s tail and, with helpers, killed it for its skin; he admits he had not learned respect. In 1897 he carried a camera, and both he and the badger fell into holes. He can laugh at himself now, and he respects the animal.
evidence: I wanted his skin, and I had not learned to respect his exemplary life and dauntless spirit.
For a moment we both looked very foolish

questions.prompt: How might a badger and a coyote become partners? Which parts of Seton’s explanation are guesses?
facilitatorNotes: The coyote follows the digging badger to catch ground-squirrels that bolt out of the back door, and the badger gets used to it. “Probable,” “no doubt” and “I do not know” mark guesses; what observers actually saw was the two travelling together.
evidence: This is the probable history of a typical case
More than one observer has seen a Badger and a Coyote travelling together

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: Chink’s great catch, and a squirrel in disguise (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Enjoy a comic story told with a straight face, then notice the writer turn from fun to a fact that surprises him.
readings.focus: A puppy who does everything wrong finally catches a picket-pin, and a striped ground-squirrel turns out not to be what it looks like.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Chink was a young dog in Seton’s camp in Yellowstone in 1897. A picket-pin ground-squirrel sits bolt upright by its hole like a picket-pin, the wooden peg used to tie up a horse. A tussock is a clump of grass; derisive means mocking; livery is a uniform; incontrovertible means impossible to argue with; omnivorous means eating both plants and animals.
readings.contentNote: The dog’s name, Chink, is also an ethnic slur against Chinese people; it is printed here as Seton wrote it. Chink’s master blames his clumsiness on “a streak of Irish,” an old joke at the expense of Irish people. A ground-squirrel eats a young mouse.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “The Squirrel and His Jerky-tail Brothers,” from “Chink and the Picket-pins” through “The Ground-squirrel That Pretends It’s a Chipmunk”; opens “As already noted in the Coyote chapter, we had in camp that summer the little dog called…”; closes “…insignia of a grain-eater, yet ruthlessly indulging in such a bloody and cannibal feast.”.

questions.prompt: Describe Chink’s way of hunting. Where does it go wrong every time?
facilitatorNotes: He begins a careful stalk far away, gets too excited to crawl, stands up and walks, then charges barking just when he should be most careful. The squirrel waits, dives, and kicks sand into his open mouth.
evidence: doing everything wrong end first, as usual
throwing with its hind feet a lot of sand right into Chink's eager, open mouth

questions.prompt: “Perseverance, he seemed to believe, must surely win in the end, as indeed it did.” How is the ending a joke? Do you believe a dog can feel foolish?
facilitatorNotes: He finally catches a picket-pin, but a wooden one. Seton says anyone who doubts a dog knows it has made a fool of itself should have seen Chink sneak behind the tent. That is Seton’s reading of the dog’s behaviour; readers can decide whether it is evidence.
evidence: actually caught his victim
he sheepishly sneaked out of sight behind the tent

questions.prompt: Why does Seton say the striped Golden Ground-squirrel is “not a Chipmunk at all”? What decides the question?
facilitatorNotes: Its coat, stripes and manners look like a chipmunk’s, but its skull and body show it is a ground-squirrel. Looks can mislead; the evidence inside settles it.
evidence: the incontrovertible evidence of its inner life, as indicated by skull and makeup

questions.prompt: Why does the story of the ground-squirrel eating a mouse give Seton “an unpleasant sensation”? Is his feeling fair to the animal?
facilitatorNotes: It looks like “innocence personified” and like a seed-eater, so the meat-eating shocks him; he even jokes that the mouse was bad-tempered. But the animal is simply omnivorous. His feeling comes from what he expected, which links back to Chink, who was also fooled by appearances.
evidence: in appearance, innocence personified
it gives one an unpleasant sensation

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the ghost rabbit (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Read a dog’s barking as Seton does, and separate what happened from what it seemed to mean.
readings.focus: A trained hound runs in terror from a white rabbit, and a shy hare grows tame where it is protected.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Before he went west, Seton lived in Ontario, Canada. A hound follows animals by scent; to tree an animal is to chase it up a tree; to bay is to bark long and deep; falsetto means high-pitched. An albino animal is born without colouring, so it is white. A cottontail is a common rabbit, and a jackrabbit is a hare. Narrow-gauge railways had small tracks, so a “narrow-gauge mule” is a small one. The mark [C] points to Seton’s note at the end of the chapter, which says the white rabbit later proved to be a tame rabbit gone wild.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “The Rabbits and Their Habits,” from “The Ghost Rabbit” through “A Narrow-gauge Mule--The Prairie Hare”; opens “An entirely different side of Rabbit life is seen in another mysterious incident that I…”; closes “…in the winter, when the snow mantle of his range might otherwise make it too conspicuous.”.

questions.prompt: How could Seton tell from the hound’s barking what animal it was following?
facilitatorNotes: A deep, strong bark at regular intervals meant a fox; a broken, uncertain one meant a rabbit; a high yelp meant the animal was treed. He listened the way a person reads a report.
evidence: The hound's bark for a Fox was deep, strong, and at regular intervals
But for a Rabbit it was broken, uncertain, irregular

questions.prompt: Seton writes the dog’s barks as words, “Rabbit, Rabbit, Rabbit” and then “Police! Help! Murder!” What does this show about what happened?
facilitatorNotes: The dog goes in confidently and comes out in a panic, hiding behind Seton’s legs. The joking translation makes the sudden change easy to hear.
evidence: shrieking, "Police! Help! Murder!"
cowering up against my legs

questions.prompt: Seton says Ranger acted “as though he thought that he had seen a ghost.” Is that something Seton observed, or his interpretation? What else might explain it?
facilitatorNotes: He observed the dog fleeing and cowering; the ghost is his interpretation, offered as a joke. An animal that looked and smelled unlike any rabbit Ranger knew could have startled him. Seton admits he never explained it, though his footnote later identified the rabbit.
evidence: Dogs are not supposed to be superstitious
that I have never been able to explain

questions.prompt: What is unusual about the prairie hares near the Mammoth Hot Springs Hotel, and what does Seton think explains it?
facilitatorNotes: Everywhere else he found them the wildest of hares, but here two let him photograph them from thirty feet, and the species had become common. He credits the protection the park gave them.
evidence: At a distance of thirty feet they gave me good chances to take pictures
Another evidence of the efficacy of protection.

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: the dangerous night visitor (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how the same event happens three times and grows more frightening each time.
readings.focus: A range bull, maddened by the smell of blood, keeps coming back to the camp in the night.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Earlier that day, camping in the Sierra mountains of California, Seton had milked a half-wild range cow while cowboys held her with ropes. The milk had blood in it, so the cowboys poured it out near the camp. Range cattle roam free and are hardly tame. A portentous sound warns of something bad; brawn is muscle; to admonish is to scold; “bluggy” is a joking baby-word for bloody; side arms are pistols.
readings.contentNote: A bull walks through the sleeping camp; at the end the cowboys seem to shoot it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “Sneak-cats--Big and Small,” the section “The Dangerous Night Visitor,” whole; opens “That night about sundown, just as we finished supper, there came from the near prairie…”; closes “…the boys came back and said, "well, you bet he won't be here again," I believed them.”.

questions.prompt: The bull comes three times. How does each visit come closer and grow more frightening?
facilitatorNotes: First it paws the ground where the milk was spilt, at the edge of the trees; then it strides into camp in the moonlight; at midnight it walks between the beds and the wagon. Each time the cowboys drive it off, and each time it returns nearer.
evidence: there was the monster at the place where that evil milk was spilt
he walked down the narrow space between our beds and the wagon

questions.prompt: Why does Seton lie still instead of jumping up when the bull walks past his bed?
facilitatorNotes: A startled bull, angry or scared, might trample them; a horse would step over a sleeper, but a bull will not. He waits until it has passed and then yells for help. Knowing animals keeps him safe.
evidence: Had I jumped up and yelled, he, whether mad or scared, might have trampled one or other of us.
That is the bull of it; a horse steps over.

questions.prompt: How does Seton make you hear the bull? Find two different ways he writes its sound.
facilitatorNotes: He describes it (“portentous rumbling roar,” “deep, vibrating organ tone,” a bellow that runs along the ground and makes his legs shake) and he spells it out: “Row-ow-ow-ow.” Feeling the sound through the ground makes it more frightening.
evidence: that deep, vibrating organ tone
that ponderous bellow running along the ground

questions.prompt: “I asked no questions.” What do you think happened to the bull, and why doesn’t Seton say so directly?
facilitatorNotes: The “pop, pop” of pistols and “he won't be here again” suggest the cowboys shot it. Seton leaves it unsaid, perhaps because he did not like it, or because the reader can work it out.
evidence: I heard the "pop, pop" of side arms
I asked no questions

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: when the bears lost their fear (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh a writer’s claim against the examples he gives, and decide who was to blame in each.
readings.focus: Years of protection make Yellowstone’s bears bold, and Seton tells what happens when people and bears forget to keep their distance.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. Fifteen years before, he had spent a day hidden by the garbage pile of a Yellowstone hotel, watching and photographing the bears that came to feed. A sanctuary is a place where animals are protected; annals are records kept year by year; a larder is a food store; a drubbing is a beating. Buffalo Jones was then in charge of the park’s wild animals. Feeding bears at the hotels was later stopped, and today visitors must stay at least 100 yards from bears in Yellowstone.
readings.contentNote: A mother bear injures a photographer; a grizzly is hauled up a tree by a rope and beaten with a club as a punishment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Bears of High and Low Degree,” the section “Further Annals of the Sanctuary,” from its opening to the grizzly sent to the Washington Zoo; opens “All of this was fifteen years ago. Since then there have been some interesting changes,…”; closes “…babies was sent to Washington Zoo, where he is now doing duty as an exhibition Grizzly.”.

questions.prompt: What does Seton mean by “the gradual removal of the restraining fear of men”? Why does it worry him?
facilitatorNotes: Protected bears stop being afraid of people, and many more now gather at once. Without that fear, he wonders, might they become a danger to the people living in the park?
evidence: the gradual removal of the restraining fear of men
as many as twenty or twenty-five Bears are now to be seen there at once

questions.prompt: Tell the camera-hunter’s story from the mother bear’s side. Why did she charge?
facilitatorNotes: He left his hiding place and crept toward her family; the cubs ran whining to her; she saw a strange “one-eyed” creature (the camera) chasing them. In her eyes he was attacking her cubs.
evidence: he decided to go to them
evidently chasing her cubs to harm them

questions.prompt: Seton says the bears had “never abused the confidence man had placed in them,” then gives exceptions. In each story, who was more to blame, the bear or the people?
facilitatorNotes: The photographer approached the cubs himself. The old grizzly learned from people that tents meant food, though he still did real damage. Readers may blame the bears, the people, or both, and should use the details.
evidence: the Bears in the Park had never abused the confidence man had placed in them
white canvas walls rising in the woods were merely invitations to a dinner ready and waiting

questions.prompt: Was Buffalo Jones’s punishment of the grizzly a good idea? What could a bear learn from a beating?
facilitatorNotes: Seton tells it as a famous feat with a lasso. The bear might learn to fear people again, or nothing at all; another grizzly was simply sent to a zoo. Today parks keep food away from bears instead. Readers can disagree.
evidence: he received a drubbing that has become famous in the moving-picture world
Another of these big, spoiled babies was sent to Washington Zoo

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: my friend the coyote (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate what a naturalist observed from the human qualities he gives an animal.
readings.focus: Seton introduces the clever coyote, the stories people tell about it, and the hungry family it hunts for.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1897 he spent a season in Yellowstone National Park, where most animals were protected from hunting. The Wild West was the American frontier, west of the Mississippi River; the prairie-dog is a kind of ground-squirrel that lives in colonies called dog-towns; Livingstone (now spelled Livingston) and Gardiner are towns in Montana on the way to the Park. Exemplary means setting a good example; attributes are qualities; in the Arabian Nights, a ruler walks among his people in disguise; a game preserve is land kept for hunting; precincts are the edges of a place; a cyclone cellar is an underground shelter from storms. Seton says the word coyote means “halfbreed”; in fact it comes from coyotl, the animal’s name in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. Since Seton wrote, coyotes have spread across nearly all of North America, eastern cities included, and today all the Park’s wild animals, coyotes too, are protected.
readings.contentNote: Seton uses “halfbreed,” an insulting old word for a person of mixed race. He speaks of “the Indians” as one group; many Native American nations tell their own stories of Coyote as a trickster or a maker of the world.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “The Cute Coyote,” the section “An Exemplary Little Beast, My Friend the Coyote,” whole; opens “If you draw a line around the region that is, or was, known as the Wild West, you will…”; closes “…level, and, if all is still, will softly hop out and in due course, resume their feeding.”.

questions.prompt: Where is the “kingdom of the Coyote,” and where does Seton see and hear it?
facilitatorNotes: The whole Wild West. He sees coyotes from the train among the prairie-dog towns along the river, sees them in the Park nearly every day, and hears them every night. (They live in the East as well now.)
evidence: you will find that you have exactly outlined the kingdom of the Coyote
This is one of the few wild creatures that you can see from the train.

questions.prompt: Seton gives three reasons why the coyote was not protected in the Park. What are they? Do you agree with them?
facilitatorNotes: It can protect itself, there are already too many, and it kills the animals it can overpower. Then, protecting wildlife meant protecting the animals people liked; today the Park protects hunters like the coyote too, because they belong in a healthy wild place. Readers can judge each reason.
evidence: first that he is so well able to protect himself, second he is even already too numerous, third he is so destructive among the creatures that he can master.

questions.prompt: People have called the coyote God’s dog, the Devil, and the Creator in disguise. What about the coyote could lead to such different ideas?
facilitatorNotes: Its cunning makes it seem more than an ordinary animal, so it can look like a helper, a troublemaker, or a hidden maker having fun. Many Native American stories show Coyote as a trickster who is clever and foolish at once.
evidence: He is a beast of rare cunning; some of the Indians call him God's dog or Medicine dog.
make the Coyote the Creator himself seeking amusement in disguise among his creatures

questions.prompt: Seton calls the coyote “an exemplary and moral little beast.” Why? Is “moral” a fair word for an animal?
facilitatorNotes: Coyote pairs stay together, and mother and father both hunt to feed their pups. Seton praises them by human standards. Some readers will say animals act by instinct, not by choosing right and wrong; others will say loyalty looks like loyalty in any creature.
evidence: For the Coyote is an exemplary and moral little beast who has only one wife
Father and mother must hunt continually and successfully to furnish their daily food.

questions.prompt: Prairie-dogs bark at an express train twenty feet away but dive underground when a coyote is far off. Why? Predict how a pair of coyotes might use this habit.
facilitatorNotes: They have learned which things hunt them; the train never does. A good prediction: one coyote shows itself and strolls away while the other hides near a hole and waits for the prairie-dog to come out. (The next section of the book tells what really happens.)
evidence: will sit up and bark at an express train but twenty feet away
downstairs they stay in the cyclone cellar until after a long interval of quiet

readings.title: Wild Animals at Home: merry Yek-yek, the prairie-dog (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Catch a writer’s jokes and doubts, and decide what he really thinks.
readings.focus: The prairie-dog has enemies everywhere and almost no pleasures, yet Seton finds it fat and merry.
readings.context: Ernest Thompson Seton (1860–1946) was a naturalist, artist and storyteller who lived in Canada and the United States. Wild Animals at Home (first published 1913) tells of animals he watched, mostly in the American and Canadian West. In 1897 he spent a season in Yellowstone National Park, where animals were protected from hunting. Livingstone (now spelled Livingston) and Gardiner are towns in Montana, north of the Park; General George S. Anderson was in charge of the Park in the 1890s. The Buffalo is the American bison, which once covered the plains in vast herds. A dunce is a slow learner; alfalfa is a crop grown to feed animals; sustenance is food; to regale is to entertain; a sentry is a guard; worthies is a joking word for important persons; “the fittest survives” means the strongest wins; per annum means each year; medieval means of the Middle Ages; retaliation is striking back; unsucculent means dry, not juicy; philosophic here means calm and wise about life. Since Seton wrote, poisoning and disease have destroyed most prairie-dog towns. Scientists now value prairie-dogs, because their digging and grazing help many other animals, burrowing owls among them, and some kinds are protected.
readings.contentNote: Seton describes farmers poisoning whole prairie-dog towns, and owls, snakes and prairie-dogs eating one another’s young.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “The Prairie-dog and His Kin,” the section “Merry Yek-yek and His Life of Troubles,” whole; opens “The common Prairie-dog is typical of the West, more so than the Buffalo is, and its…”; closes “…power to discover happiness within in spite of all the cold unfriendly world about him.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the prairie-dog called a “dog”? What joke do old-timers make about its voice and its tail?
facilitatorNotes: Its alarm call sounds like a bark, though it is really a ground-squirrel. Because it jerks up its tail every time it calls, they joke that its voice is “tied to its tail.” The joke rests on a real observation.
evidence: The absurd name "dog" having been given on account of its "bark."
every time it "yeks" it jerks up its tail

questions.prompt: Old books told of the prairie-dog, the owl and the rattlesnake living together as partners. What does Seton think really happens? How does he show his doubt?
facilitatorNotes: The owl and snake use holes the prairie-dog has left, and when two of them meet, the stronger wins; each may eat the others’ young. He tells the partnership story in grand business words, then adds a dry “This is pleasing if true.”
evidence: This is pleasing if true.
if any two of the three underground worthies happen to meet in the same hole, the fittest survives.

questions.prompt: Seton calls poisoning prairie-dogs a “medieval Italian mode.” What does that phrase suggest about his opinion?
facilitatorNotes: It links farmers with old stories of Italian poisoners, so it sounds disapproving, though he never argues against the farmers directly. The next words, “Poor helpless little Yek-yek,” show where his sympathy lies. Readers can also weigh the farmers’ side: the damage to their crops was real.
evidence: which medieval Italian mode has become the accepted method in the West.
Farmers consider Prairie-dogs a great nuisance

questions.prompt: How does Seton make you feel sorry for Yek-yek? Where does he exaggerate for fun?
facilitatorNotes: Every hunter is his enemy, he cannot fight back, and his only pleasure is a hurried meal of dry grass. The joke that he has dodged down his hole so often that his ears are worn off is an exaggeration: prairie-dogs simply have small ears.
evidence: The prey of everything that preys, he yet seems incapable of any measure of retaliation.
his ears are worn off close to his head

questions.prompt: Yek-yek is still “fat and merry.” How does Seton explain it? Do you think an animal can be happy, or is Seton giving it human feelings?
facilitatorNotes: Seton says it must have a “philosophic power” to find happiness inside itself. One defensible view: an animal can be healthy and lively without thinking about its troubles, so “merry” may be Seton’s human word for that. Others may think animals really do feel something like happiness.
evidence: Yet he is fat and merry; undoubtedly he enjoys his every day on earth
a philosophic power to discover happiness within
